newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir engineer realigns station, lights back on.
newsitem.headline: Mir engineer realigns station, lights back on.

text.p: Russia's troubled Mir space station has been realigned to face the Sun and the lights are back on in the sprawling orbital craft, Russian and American officials said on Friday.
"We solved the problem," NASA official Mark Severance told Reuters at Russian Mission Control outside Moscow. "Things are going real well."
Flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin toiled through the night on Mir and most systems were reconnected.

Systems crashed on Thursday when a cable was accidentally unplugged, a further blow to a mission already dogged by problems. A cargo tug hit the station last month, holing a module and sparking the worst crisis in Mir's 11-year history.

A senior Russian Mission Control official who declined to be identified said the gyrodines, devices which reorient the station without the need to use precious fuel, would be reconnected later on Friday.

The remaining systems would be switched on after that. This would restore Mir to the condition it was in before Thursday, meaning the repairs to the punctured Spektr module would still be outstanding. It was not clear when they would be carried out.
"They have fully set up the orientation," the official said. "The electrical systems are gathering energy from the Sun."

Mission commander Vladimir Tsibliyev, who fell ill with a heart problem earlier in the week, and British-born NASA astronaut Michael Foale went to bed around 2000 GMT while Lazutkin carried on working until around 0030 GMT.
He reconnected power systems in the main body of Mir, including oxygen, life support systems and the lights, before getting some sleep himself, the officials said.
Russian space experts met at 0500 GMT to discuss the next steps in the repair plan. Around the same time, Mir passed over an area of Russia close to Moscow on its orbit around the globe.
"They want to give the crew a few days off before they resume work," Severance said.
